title: warpdotdev/warp — Warp is an agentic development environment, born out of the terminal.
content:
Website · Code · Agents · Terminal · Drive · Docs · How Warp Works
Note
OpenAI is the founding sponsor of the new, open-source Warp repository, and the new agentic management workflows are powered by GPT models.
Warp is an agentic development environment, born out of the terminal. Use Warp's built-in coding agent, or bring your own CLI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and others).
You can download Warp and read our docs for platform-specific instructions.
Explore build.warp.dev to:
- Watch thousands of Oz agents triage issues, write specs, implement changes, and review PRs
- View top contributors and in-flight features
- Track your own issues with GitHub sign-in
- Click into active agent sessions in a web-compiled Warp terminal
Maintaining a popular open-source project? Apply for Oz credits to explore Oz for OSS.
Oz for OSS is our partner program for bringing the same agentic open-source management workflows used in this repository to select partner repositories. We work directly with maintainers to implement workflows for issue triage, PR review, community management, and contributor coordination in a way that fits each project.
Warp's UI framework (the warpui_core and warpui crates) are licensed under the MIT license.
The rest of the code in this repository is licensed under the AGPL v3.
Warp's client codebase is open source and lives in this repository. We welcome community contributions and have designed a lightweight workflow to help new contributors get started. For the full contribution flow, read our CONTRIBUTING.md guide.
Tip
Chat with contributors and the Warp team in the #oss-contributors Slack channel — a good place for ad-hoc questions, design discussion, and pairing with maintainers. New here? Join the Warp Slack community first, then jump into #oss-contributors.
Before filing, search existing issues for your bug or feature request. If nothing exists, file an issue using our templates. Security vulnerabilities should be reported privately as described in CONTRIBUTING.md.
Once filed, a Warp maintainer reviews the issue and may apply a readiness label: ready-to-spec signals the design is open for contributors to spec out, and ready-to-implement signals the design is settled and code PRs are welcome. Anyone can pick up a labeled issue — mention @oss-maintainers on an issue if you'd like it considered for a readiness label.
To build and run Warp from source:
./script/bootstrap   # platform-specific setup
./script/run         # build and run Warp
./script/presubmit   # fmt, clippy, and tests
See AGENTS.md for the full engineering guide, including coding style, testing, and platform-specific notes.
Interested in joining the team? See our open roles.
- See our docs for a comprehensive guide to Warp's features.
- Join our Slack Community to connect with other users and get help from the Warp team — contributors hang out in #oss-contributors .
- Try our Preview build to test the latest experimental features.
- Mention @oss-maintainers on any issue to escalate to the team — for example, if you encounter problems with the automated agents.
We ask everyone to be respectful and empathetic. Warp follows the Code of Conduct. To report violations, email warp-coc at warp.dev.
We'd like to call out a few of the open source dependencies that have helped Warp to get off the ground:

report.summary: Warp open-sources its agentic development environment—a terminal-based platform where AI agents code, triage issues, and maintain projects, with OpenAI as founding sponsor.
report.background: Warp began as a modern, GPU-accelerated terminal emulator, but has evolved into an 'agentic development environment' that places AI agents at the center of software workflows. The new repository is open-sourced with OpenAI as its founding sponsor, and its agentic management workflows are powered by GPT models. Warp supports both its built-in coding agent and external CLI agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI, making it a versatile hub rather than a locked-in assistant. The company also runs Oz, a fleet of agents that triage issues, write specs, implement changes, and review pull requests across the repository. By open-sourcing the client codebase—UI framework crates under MIT, the rest under AGPL v3—Warp hopes to attract community contributors and extend similar agentic workflows to other open-source projects through its Oz for OSS program.
key_points: Warp transforms the traditional terminal into an agentic development environment. It includes a built-in coding agent, but also supports integrating external CLI agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI, letting developers mix and match AI assistants in one workflow. This flexibility makes it an open platform rather than a locked-in tool.

OpenAI is the founding sponsor of Warp's new open-source repository. Agentic management workflows—including issue triage, spec writing, implementation, and PR review—are powered by GPT models, signaling deeper collaboration between terminal startups and major AI labs. The build.warp.dev portal lets anyone watch thousands of these Oz agents in action.

The repository uses split licensing: Warp's UI framework (warpui_core and warpui crates) is MIT-licensed, while the rest of the code falls under AGPL v3. This open-sourcing invites community contributions, with a designed lightweight workflow for new contributors. The client codebase lives entirely in the repository, and maintainers use readiness labels such as ready-to-spec and ready-to-implement to guide contributions.

Warp's 'Oz for OSS' partner program provides open-source maintainers with credits and specialized agent workflows. These agents handle issue triage, PR review, community management, and contributor coordination, tailored to each project's needs. The goal is to bring the same agentic open-source management workflows used in Warp's own repository to select partner projects.

Building from source requires running ./script/bootstrap, ./script/run, and ./script/presubmit. An AGENTS.md engineering guide covers coding style, testing, and platform-specific notes, lowering the barrier for contributors. The community coordinates via Slack, primarily in the #oss-contributors channel, where maintainers and newcomers can discuss design and pair on contributions.
report.impact: Warp's open-source, terminal-based agentic environment gives developers a flexible hub for AI-assisted development. By supporting multiple CLI agents, it reduces vendor lock-in and positions the terminal as a neutral orchestration layer. For the AI industry, this signals a shift from single-agent editors to multi-agent open platforms, with OpenAI's sponsorship highlighting commercial investment in open source. Developers benefit from transparent contribution workflows and can inspect the actual agent management code. For regular users and OSS maintainers, Oz agents promise to automate tedious maintenance tasks, potentially accelerating project velocity—though AGPL licensing and reliance on GPT models raise governance and cost considerations.
report.tools: Watch the Warp repository (github.com/warpdotdev/warp) and its build.warp.dev dashboard for live Oz agent activity. Explore the AGENTS.md engineering guide and the warpui_core/warpui crates. For agent integration, follow Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI. If maintaining an OSS project, apply for Oz for OSS credits.
